name: Thomas William Burgess
highlight: Second successful Channel swimmer · 22 hours 35 minutes
biography: Thomas William ‘Bill’ Burgess was an English swimmer, Olympic competitor and coach, born in Rotherham on 15 June 1872. He settled in Paris and represented the French club Libellule de Paris at the 1900 Olympics while retaining British nationality. His Olympic programme included fourth place in the 4,000 metres freestyle and a bronze medal in water polo.

After years of unsuccessful Channel attempts, Burgess completed the England-to-France crossing on 5–6 September 1911 in 22 hours and 35 minutes. He became the second person to succeed, 36 years after Matthew Webb. He departed from South Foreland and arrived at Le Chatelet, accompanied by the motorboat Elsie and rowing boat Orchid.

Burgess subsequently helped other swimmers prepare for the Channel. His pupils included Gertrude Ederle, whose 1926 crossing made her the first successful woman, and several further pioneers. His contribution therefore extended from his own endurance achievement to the development of later Channel swimmers.

lines.text: Burgess followed Matthew Webb as the second successful swimmer. The published witness declaration records a shore-to-shore swim without boat contact, with nourishment supplied in the water. A contemporary report reproduces Burgess’s account of using overarm sidestroke with some backstroke. It names Weidman as a companion swimmer and describes rowing support after motorboat wash became troublesome.
The witness declaration gives 5–6 September and 22h35m; the museum’s surrounding narrative instead prints 8 September. The date inconsistency remains unresolved.

lines.text: CSA record 2462 supplies name, England, direction and 22:35. Dover Museum publishes the witness declaration supplying the departure, arrival, clocks and support craft. Its narrative date conflicts with that declaration. AthRecs has inspected the published transcription, not the original document in person. The Poverty Bay Herald’s London-datelined report of 8 September, published 11 October 1911, separately gives 22h35m and attributes the stroke account to Burgess. Its publicly available transcription was inspected; the original scan was not legible or available for confirmation.
